newsitem.title: BELGIUM: U.S. works on nuclear deal with Russia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. works on nuclear deal with Russia.

text.p: Washington will offer Moscow a deal cutting the huge U.S. advantage in sea-based strategic nuclear missiles as part of efforts to win Russian support for NATO plans to expand eastwards, alliance sources said on Thursday.

They said U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott, Washington's point man on relations with Russia, had taken the proposals to Moscow on Thursday after conferring closely with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana.
Solana held five hours of talks with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on Monday in the first official negotiating session on new post-Cold War relations between NATO and Russia.

Solana, who formally offered the Russians a permanent consultative mechanism, hinted at concessions on outstanding arms control issues and more generous financial help to President Boris Yeltsin's government.

But Solana, who speaks for all 16 alliance countries, is not mandated to negotiate the clearly linked but highly sensitive issue of U.S.-Russia arms control agreements -- strictly a bilateral subject.
"START-3 (Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty-3) was not mentioned, but the secretary-general realises fully well it is part of a wider package," said one NATO source.

Russia adamantly opposes NATO's plans to enlarge into former communist central and eastern Europe later this year. Solana's talks with Primakov simply underlined the differences between the two sides.
NATO is adamant that the new members, certain to include Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, will be named at a special summit in Madrid in July.

But in parallel with enlargement they want a new deal with Russia without which the spread of stability in Europe -- the most-frequently voiced justification for enlargement -- is seriously undermined.
Moscow argues that alliance expansion into countries which currently face no threat from either east or west will simply create new divisions in Europe and put back cooperation in other areas.

In the present climate, NATO diplomats say START-2, a landmark arms control treaty reducing the huge land-based nuclear arsenals of the Cold War, has no chance of being ratified by the Russian parliament.
"Everyone sees that START-2 will not go through at the moment," said one diplomat.

Apart from giving away a major negotiating point, the Russians fear ratification would simply freeze the huge superiority the United States currently has in sea-borne missiles carried by its submarine fleet.

The U.S. administration, under the watchful eye of a Congress still suspicious of Russia, cannot scrap its own missiles until START-2 is ratified -- forcing it to spend billions of dollars maintaining unneeded weapons' systems.

NATO diplomats say Washington is prepared to offer a "framework agreement" on a START-3, reducing sea-borne missiles, but would tie it to ratification of START-2 and a number of other "carrots" in an eventual NATO-Russia pact.
The details are expected to be thrashed out at a meeting in Washington on February 5-6 between Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and U.S. Vice-President Al Gore.
The deal could then be endorsed at a planned March summit between Presidents Boris Yeltsin and Bill Clinton.
